newsitem.title: USA: Culture crimps air cargo perishable shipments.
newsitem.headline: Culture crimps air cargo perishable shipments.

text.p: Cultural differences may be a big hurdle for the air cargo industry in trying to boost perishables shipping around the global village, a recent workshop revealed.
"There are always 1,001 excuses (from the growers)", said one executive for a cargo airline that serves Latin America.

A gathering here of perishables shipping executives sponsored by the Frankfurt and Miami airports identified some pitfalls in boosting perishable traffic between the two airports, but strategies to begin solving the problems will probably take many more meetings.

Reliability was a major point of discussion. "The on time rate of the cargo airlines serving Latin America is 40 percent, compared with 97 percent for Federal Express and 85 percent for passenger airlines," discussion leader Manuel Aragon, director of Teqflor Inc. Miami, said.

The cargo airlines complained that the growers of flowers, fruits and vegetables and fishermen have problems making departure times. Then the perishable cargo does not arrive at Miami International Airport (MIA) in time to make its connection to Europe.
"Should they (the airlines) take off and leave somebody behind?" asked Aragon, even if the no-show represents 50 percent of the cargo?
Several European representatives recommended the cargo simply be left behind. "If you leave the freight back one or two times, they will be on time the next time," said one European delegate.

"It is all very easy for us to sit here - we can pick up the phone and it always works, the fax always goes through - and make the rules for how they should work 'down there,'" countered one floral distributor.

The stakes are high for both airports, which have big perishables businesses. In fact, perishables are MIA's biggest cargo. In 1995 flowers were MIA's biggest single commodity by weight with 167,000 tons and fish was second with 93,000 tons, according to the most recent statistics compiled by the Metro-Dade County Aviation Department.

Others pointed out that customs agencies in Latin America are nortorious for causing delays. "If the paperwork is not just exactly right, some customs will not allow you to unload the aircraft," said one carrier.
"If you cannot unload the aircraft for several hours, then it delays the loading as well," he said.
Still other blamed maintenance delays of the often aging freighter fleet.
"We need proper airport facilities in Latin America," said one, "sometimes they are palletising right there on the tarmac."

The participants all agreed that much more standarization is needed. "We need standard box sizes for flowers and marking of the boxes. If there are 1,000 farms worldwide, there are probably 1,000 labels for the product," said one participant.
Another urged some standards for the produce. "Someone will complain that the roses are too open, can we measure that?"
The airports are working to schedule another perishables meeting in Frankfurt.
